Back to home

Making dementia care more connected, consistent and human.

A care coordination system designed to help families and caregivers stay connected, share updates and maintain continuity in the everyday care of people living with dementia.

The Problem

People living with dementia need consistent, familiar and reassuring support in their daily lives, while family members and professional caregivers lack a shared system to coordinate routines, communicate care-related information and maintain continuity across caregiving transitions.

Why does this need to exist?

Rise In Nuclear Families

Work, opportunity and changing living arrangements mean adult children may live separately from their ageing parents.

Shift to Professional Care

When dementia or other health conditions require regular support, families may bring in professional caregivers to help manage everyday care.

Care is no longer always managed by one person. It can become a shared responsibility across a wider care network for such individuals with dementia.

Where communication breaks down.

When dementia care is shared between family members and professional caregivers, important updates and observations can get lost.

01 –

Missed handovers

Daily observations and routine updates don't always reach the next caregiver.

02 –

Lack of visibility

Family members may struggle to know what happens when they aren't around.

03 –

Fragmented care information

Important details about routines, behaviour and wellbeing can remain scattered across people.

For someone living with dementia these gaps can make the condition even worse.

02Understanding the problem

What is actually breaking down in everyday care?

I looked at three sources: what families share online, what research says about dementia, and what the people giving care told me.

What I Found in Online Dementia Care Communities

Secondary research

Understanding dementia beyond memory loss.

Dementia affects more than memory. It can influence orientation, communication, behaviour and the ability to carry out everyday activities.

Stage 01

Mild Alzheimer's

  • Short-term memory loss
  • Confusion about time
  • Repeated questions
  • Difficulty following conversations

Stage 02

Moderate Alzheimer's

  • Difficulty recognising familiar people or relationships
  • Increased disorientation
  • Difficulty with multi-step tasks
  • Behavioural changes

Stage 03

Severe Alzheimer's

  • Significant memory loss
  • Limited verbal communication
  • Reduced motor control
  • Need for constant care

EarlyProgressive

Secondary research

What literature told me.

I reviewed 10–12 research papers alongside online articles, blogs and posts.

01.

The power of familiarity

Familiar faces, voices, personal objects and routines can provide reassurance. Long-term and emotional memories may remain relatively accessible even when recent recall becomes difficult, particularly in early-stage Alzheimer's.

Sources

  • Alzheimer's Association, 2023
  • Lim et al., 2018
  • Cohen-Mansfield, 2001
  • NICE Guidelines, 2018

02.

Non-pharmacological interventions

Cognitive stimulation, reminiscence and life-story activities can be incorporated into everyday interactions rather than being limited to formal clinical sessions.

Sources

  • Berg-Weger, 2017, Non-Pharmacologic Interventions for Persons with Dementia

03.

Caregiver burden

Fragmented caregiving, poor coordination, lack of shared visibility and emotional fatigue affect both family and professional caregivers.

Sources

  • Alzheimer's Disease International, 2019
  • Bangerter et al., 2017

Primary research

Talking to the people involved.

Next I ran contextual interviews with 3 family caregivers and 2 mental health professionals, a college psychologist and a practising psychiatrist. I asked them to walk me through a normal day. The same worries came up again and again.

Key research insights

Dementia isn't just hard for the patient. It breaks the entire family system.

From the outside, dementia looks like a memory problem. But once I got into the field, the real picture was more complex. The families I observed weren't struggling because of memory loss alone — they were struggling because care was disorganized, invisible, and held together by improvisation. Caregivers changed through the day with no handover. Family members worked full-time with no visibility. Information was stored in people's heads, not systems.

Pain point 01

Fragmented, Shift-Based Care

Multiple caregivers work in rotation with no structured handovers. Critical information — routines, behaviors, medication — gets lost between shifts.

Pain point 02

No Tracking System Exists

Daily care — meals, medications, tasks — is tracked verbally or not at all. There is no log, no history, no ground truth anyone can rely on.

Pain point 03

Families Are Anxious and Invisible

Working family members can't be present. They have no window into daily care. Some families resort to CCTV just to see what's happening with their parent.

Pain point 04

Communication is Informal and Unreliable

Caregiver handovers happen on WhatsApp or phone calls — unstructured, unsearchable, and easy to miss. The care team is never truly aligned.

Pain point 05

Routine Breaks Down Constantly

Different caregivers follow different routines. For dementia patients, inconsistency isn't just inconvenient — it directly causes confusion and distress.

Pain point 06

The Emotional Toll is Invisible

Families carry the weight of caregiving on top of work and life. There's no support built into existing systems for the people doing the caring.

→Next, I mapped who is involved and where these breakdowns happen.

Flow model

The people around Ramesh.

What it showed

Most breakdowns sit between people: shift changes with no follow-up, no formal handover, and monitoring that gets fuzzy when the family is busy.

→

What it changed

User scenarios

Everyday moments that break down

Real situations from the care journey that show where communication, continuity and information often fall apart.

01.

Checking on the
morning dose

Chitra ThakurFamily member
Nandha KumariProfessional carer
  1. Remembers the morning tablet during a meeting
  2. Messages the carer to check
  3. Waits for a reply
  4. Gets a half answer
  5. Calls again at lunch

Insight

Show what's already done, at a glance, so nobody has to call to ask.

02.

Changing
shifts

Nandha KumariProfessional carer
  1. The previous carer leaves in a hurry
  2. Gets a quick verbal update
  3. Misses one instruction
  4. A task is repeated or skipped

Insight

The record itself should be the handover, so nothing depends on memory.

03.

The doctor's
visit

Chitra ThakurFamily member
  1. Takes Ramesh for his check-up
  2. The doctor asks how the last month went
  3. Tries to remember from calls and messages
  4. Forgets about the bad nights

Insight

The doctor needs a short summary of the weeks since the last visit, not a phone full of messages.

What do they want?

Different needs, same goal

Both family members and professional caregivers want the same thing: to provide the best possible care. But their needs, routines and challenges are different.

They want visibility, reassurance and control.

Primary user

Family members

  • Know what's done without calling
  • Peace of mind while at work
  • Coordinate carers easily
  • Stay emotionally connected

They want clarity, simplicity and trust.

Secondary user

Professional carers

  • Clear instructions for every task
  • An easy way to mark tasks done
  • Know what the last shift did
  • Keep the family's trust

→This gave me a clear problem to design for.

04How might we

The main question

How might we help families and professional caregivers coordinate everyday dementia care, maintain consistent routines and stay informed about a person's well-being?

HMW 01

How might we support memory recall and familiarity for people with early-to-mid-stage dementia during everyday interactions?

HMW 02

How might we reduce anxiety and emotional distress caused by confusion, recognition gaps and fragmented care?

HMW 03

How might we ensure daily care activities are clearly tracked across multiple caregivers?

HMW 04

How might we provide family members visibility into daily care without being physically present?

→These questions decided which features made it into the app.

Roles

One system, three roles.

Family members and professional caregivers work in the same space and see the same record.

In the final screens

Family organiser

Sets up the circle, assigns and reassigns tasks, adds medicine, invites people and follows the timeline.

In shared screens

Professional caregiver

Receives assigned tasks with reminders, marks them done, and posts comments and updates to the timeline.

Proposed

Person living with dementia

Joins as the care recipient. Memories and familiar faces reach them through the people around them.

06The final experience

One shared space for the whole care circle.

The final screens follow one day in Ramesh's care circle, from a morning check-in to a new medicine that every caregiver can see.

The hero flow

One day in the care circle.

Every task carries who it is assigned to, when it is due and when it was done, so each handover starts from the same record.

Design decision · From finding 03: family members kept calling caregivers to confirm meals and medicines, so updates now come to them in the timeline.

Task 01

Setting up the care circle.

A family organiser creates an account, defines their role and sets up a care circle to monitor care activities.

Design decision · From the personas: each person in the circle has a different job, so onboarding asks for role and relationship first.

Task 03

Creating a routine task.

A new daily-routine task is created, scheduled and assigned to the care circle.

Task 04

Adding a medicine.

A medication and its dosage are added and assigned so every caregiver can track and follow it.

Design decision · From finding 03: families were unsure whether medicines had been given, so each dose has an owner and a reminder.

Task 05

Inviting family.

More people join the care circle through an SMS invitation from contacts.

07Reflection

What I'd take forward.

What I learned

  • Dementia care is a coordination problem as much as a memory problem. Field research moved my focus from memory aids to the people around the patient.
  • Small details carry trust. A timestamp, an assignee or a photo answers the question a family would otherwise call about.

Limitations

  • The research sample was small: 5 conversations with family caregivers and mental health professionals.
  • Personas are synthesised from these conversations.
  • The final screens follow the family organiser. The caregiver's shift view and the care recipient's view are still to be designed.

What I'd do next

  • Fix the four think-aloud issues: onboarding completion, contained comments, one clear add action and clearer invite labels.
  • Design the doctor's visit summary from scenario 03.
  • Test the memory features with families and people living with early-stage dementia.

The system gives every person in the care circle the same picture of the day, which keeps care consistent for the person at its centre.
